# Reading and Writing Data

:::{.callout-note title="Draft"}
First draft, 2026-10-20, from the outline of 2026-10-19. Every number in the text is computed when the book builds. Only the rounding warning in Writing needs dev dplR 1.8.1. Open questions are in the backlog.
:::

## Big Idea

A ring-width file is somebody's measurements plus their decisions about how to write them down. Most of those decisions are invisible once the file is read. The reader has to work out what the file meant, and now and then it has to guess.

Here is the one place in the book's two collections where the guess matters. The Hurricane Ridge file has a value of `-999` for the first core of tree 1 in 1900. Is that a ring of zero width, or a year nobody measured? The two answers lead to different series, and every later chapter would treat them differently. A ring of zero width is an absent ring, something that happened to the tree, and crossdating leans on it. A year with no measurement is a hole.

By the end of this chapter you can read a file, see what the reader decided for you, and write the data back out without losing anything on the way.

## Packages

```{r}
#| label: read-setup
#| message: false
library(dplR)
```

That's all. The files are the two in the book's `data/` folder, `co021.rwl` and `wa082.rwl`, exactly as the International Tree-Ring Data Bank (ITRDB) serves them. The [Data Sources](A2DataSources.qmd) appendix has the download and says where they came from.

## Reading a File

`read.rwl` is the front door. Give it a file name and it works out the format.

```{r}
#| label: read-co021
co021 <- read.rwl("data/co021.rwl")
```

It looked at the file, decided it was Tucson format, and handed it to `read.tucson`, which printed one line: `r ncol(co021)` series from `r min(time(co021))` to `r max(time(co021))`, measured to 0.01 mm. In a script I name the format. A guess that works today can go another way after somebody edits the file, and I'd rather the script stopped than read the file as something it isn't.

```{r}
#| label: read-wa082
wa082 <- read.rwl("data/wa082.rwl", format = "tucson")
```

Hurricane Ridge has more to say, and the next few sections are about that message. First, what came back?

```{r}
#| label: read-look
class(wa082)
dim(wa082)
wa082[c("1809", "1810", "1811", "1812"), 1:3]
```

A data frame with one row per year and one column per series. The years are the row names, and `time(wa082)` gives them back as numbers. A series is `NA` before its first ring and after its last, so 712011 is `NA` until 1811 and 712021 hasn't started yet. The class `rwl` on top of `data.frame` tells the rest of `dplR` that these are ring widths. The [aside on classes](04xAsideClassesGenerics.qmd) after the next chapter explains why.

Where did the 0.01 mm come from? The file says so, though not in words. A Tucson file marks the end of each series with a stop code, and the stop code sets the precision of every value in that series. The [aside on the Tucson format](03xAsideTucsonFormat.qmd) goes through the layout column by column.

## The Read Record

A reader makes decisions, so `read.tucson` writes them down. The notes travel with the data as an attribute.

```{r}
#| label: read-record
waRecord <- attr(wa082, "dplR.provenance")
names(waRecord)
waRecord$header
```

The first three lines of the file are a header in the ITRDB's layout, and the reader keeps them word for word. They hold things the ring widths can't: a site name, the species code (ABAM, Pacific silver fir), an elevation of 1560 m, the span, and who collected it. The rest of the record is the precision of each series, any series the reader renamed, any events it noticed while reading, and the gaps.

```{r}
#| label: read-record-parts
table(waRecord$precision$precision)
nrow(waRecord$renames)
nrow(waRecord$events)
waRecord$gaps
```

All `r nrow(waRecord$precision)` series are at 0.01 mm. Nothing was renamed and nothing odd turned up, except one gap.

Mesa Verde's record is shorter.

```{r}
#| label: read-record-co021
coRecord <- attr(co021, "dplR.provenance")
coRecord$header
```

No header at all. The file is ring widths and nothing else, so it can't tell you where the trees grew or which cores came from which tree. You have to get that from somewhere else, and the Data Sources appendix says what I could and couldn't check.

My advice is to keep the record with the data and read it before you trust any numbers. It is where the file's oddities end up after the read, and some of them never make it into a printed message.

## A Gap Is Not a Zero

Back to tree 1 in 1900. The file holds `-999` there, and the reader returned `NA`, with a message that says why. The file records no measurement for that year, and no measurement is not the same thing as a ring of zero width.

That is the reader's default. You can ask for zeros instead, and the older reader, `read.tucson.legacy`, gives zeros without being asked.

```{r}
#| label: read-three-ways
#| message: false
waZero <- read.tucson("data/wa082.rwl", fill.internal.NA = 0)
waLegacy <- read.tucson.legacy("data/wa082.rwl", verbose = FALSE)
waOnBoard <- local({
  data(wa082, package = "dplR", envir = environment())
  wa082
})
yrs <- as.character(1898:1902)
data.frame(
  year = yrs,
  default = wa082[yrs, "712011"],
  zero = waZero[yrs, "712011"],
  legacy = waLegacy[yrs, "712011"],
  onBoard = waOnBoard[yrs, "712011"]
)
```

The last column is the copy of Hurricane Ridge that ships with `dplR`, which was read the old way and holds a zero. Its own record says so (`attr(wa082, "dplR.provenance")$fill.internal.NA` on the on-board data is `r attr(waOnBoard, "dplR.provenance")$fill.internal.NA`).

Does it matter? One ring in one series out of `r ncol(wa082)`? Ask `rwl.check`, which looks for defects in a collection and is the subject of the next chapter.

```{r}
#| label: read-check-gap
#| message: false
rwl.check(wa082)
```

With the gap left as `NA`, you get a warning that names the year, says the file recorded nothing there, and lists the functions that will refuse the series until you deal with it. Now the same check on the copy holding a zero.

```{r}
#| label: read-check-zero
rwl.check(waOnBoard)
```

One note: a ring of zero width. Nothing about a gap. Once the hole is a zero, nothing downstream can tell it from an absent ring, and every method in the book will treat 1900 as a year in which that tree put on no wood at all. The read record still knows the zero was a gap. `rwl.check` reads the record for the reader's warnings about the file, but not for that.

Compare Mesa Verde, which has `r sum(co021 == 0, na.rm = TRUE)` zeros. Those are absent rings, recorded on purpose by people who looked for them in the wood. In an `rwl` object they look exactly like the zero in 1900 at Hurricane Ridge, and only the person who measured the cores knew which was which. That's why the reader returns `NA` by default and prints a message about it. What 1900 becomes is your call, and the message makes sure you know there is a call to make.

What to do about the gap is a choice, and it comes later in the book. The short version: it stays a gap through crossdating, and gets filled at the start of [Detrending](08Detrending.qmd), where `detrend` first refuses it.

## Trees and Cores

Series names usually carry more than a label. At Hurricane Ridge, 712011 is site 712, tree 01, core 1. `autoread.ids` works that out from the names.

```{r}
#| label: read-ids
waIds <- autoread.ids(wa082)
head(waIds)
table(table(waIds$tree))
```

`r length(unique(waIds$tree))` trees, `r sum(table(waIds$tree) == 2)` with two cores and `r sum(table(waIds$tree) == 1)` with one. You met the same function on the simulated collection in [chapter 2](02CoresToRecord.qmd), and it matters for the same reason: several statistics later in the book compare cores within a tree to cores between trees, and they need to know which is which.

The names at Mesa Verde are less obliging.

```{r}
#| label: read-ids-co021
coIds <- autoread.ids(co021)
table(table(coIds$tree))
```

It settles on `r length(unique(coIds$tree))` trees with one to four cores each, but it warns that it is unsure. When the guess is wrong, or when you know the scheme, say it with `read.ids` and the number of characters for the site, the tree and the core.

```{r}
#| label: read-ids-stc
head(read.ids(wa082, stc = c(3, 2, 1)))
```

Here that agrees with the guess. For Mesa Verde I trust the guess only as far as the correlations back it up, and the Data Sources appendix shows them.

## Other Formats

Most ring widths you will meet are in Tucson format, because the ITRDB is. Most of the rest come out of a spreadsheet, with a column of years and a column for each series. `read.sheet` reads those from a text file separated by commas, tabs, semicolons or pipes. COFECHA never read spreadsheets, and you had to convert them with another program first [@GrissinoMayer2001]. To show it without adding a file to the book, I write Mesa Verde out as a spreadsheet and read it back.

```{r}
#| label: read-sheet
sheetFile <- tempfile(fileext = ".csv")
invisible(write.sheet(co021, sheetFile))
readLines(sheetFile, n = 2)
co021Sheet <- read.sheet(sheetFile)
all.equal(co021, co021Sheet, check.attributes = FALSE)
```

The round trip gives back the same `r ncol(co021Sheet)` series with the same values. A spreadsheet has no stop codes, so there is nothing in the file to say what precision the measurements were taken at. The reader works it out from the values.

The Heidelberg format, which TSAP writes, is common in European labs, and `read.fh` reads it. There are also readers for the compact format (`read.compact`) and TRiDaS (`read.tridas`). I've seen very little data in either, and they get no example here.

`read.rwl` sits in front of all of these and passes the file to the right one.

## Writing

The writers mirror the readers: `write.tucson`, `write.sheet`, `write.compact`, `write.tridas`, and `write.rwl` in front of them. What I want from a writer is that what goes out comes back unchanged. Does Hurricane Ridge survive the trip, gap and all?

```{r}
#| label: read-write-tucson
tucsonFile <- tempfile(fileext = ".rwl")
invisible(write.tucson(wa082, tucsonFile))
grep("^712011  1900", readLines(tucsonFile), value = TRUE)
waBack <- read.tucson(tucsonFile)
all.equal(wa082, waBack, check.attributes = FALSE)
```

The gap goes out as `-999`, the first value on 712011's line for the 1900s, and comes back as `NA`. Everything else matches.

The one place a writer can lose something is precision. `write.tucson` writes at 0.01 mm unless you tell it otherwise, and it rounds whatever you give it to fit. Put a width measured to the thousandth in a series and write it at the default.

```{r}
#| label: read-write-prec
#| warning: true
waFine <- wa082
waFine["1698", "712122"] <- 0.123
fineFile <- tempfile(fileext = ".rwl")
invisible(write.tucson(waFine, fineFile))
read.tucson(fineFile, verbose = FALSE)["1698", "712122"]
invisible(write.tucson(waFine, fineFile, prec = 0.001))
read.tucson(fineFile, verbose = FALSE)["1698", "712122"]
```

At the default the 0.123 comes back as 0.12. The warning says how many values were rounded, by how much, and in which series. Up to `dplR` 1.8.0 the rounding happened without a word, so a lab that measured to the thousandth and forgot `prec` lost the third decimal place in every ring and had no way to know. At `prec = 0.001` the value survives, and the warning goes away. If your lab measures to the thousandth, write to the thousandth.

`write.tucson` can also write an ITRDB header from a list (`header =`), and the help page shows one. The help page also says not to use it for a submission to the ITRDB. The header standard is loose, and the ITRDB takes the metadata through its website. I agree with the help page.

Chronologies have their own readers and writers, `read.crn` and `write.crn`. They come up in [Chronology Building](10Chronologies.qmd), once there is a chronology to write.

## Wrapping Up

Reading a file tells you the shape of the data and what the file said about itself, and the read record keeps the parts you'd otherwise lose: the header, the precision, and any gaps. It can't tell you whether any of the years are right. A file that reads cleanly can still have a missing ring in every core. Checking the collection is the [next chapter](04CheckingCollection.qmd), and crossdating comes after that.

## Exercises

1. Read `data/wa082.rwl` with `fill.internal.NA = 0` and run `rwl.check` on it. Which finding disappears, and what took its place? Where in the object can you still find out that 1900 was a gap?
2. Write `co021` with `write.sheet`, open the file in a spreadsheet, delete one value from the middle of a series, save it, and read it back with `read.sheet`. What does the reader do with the hole, and where is it recorded?
3. Read the three header lines in the Hurricane Ridge read record. Which of them could you check against something else, and how?
4. Write `wa082` with `write.tucson(prec = 0.001)` and open the file in a text editor. What changed in the numbers, and what changed at the end of each series?

## Further Reading

Grissino-Mayer [-@GrissinoMayer2001] is a manual and tutorial for COFECHA, and COFECHA is where a lot of people first meet the Tucson format. Its short section on data formats says what the DPL programs read and what they couldn't, and the rest is worth reading before the crossdating chapters.

The `read.tucson` help page describes the new reader, what it does with gaps and odd layouts, and how it differs from `read.tucson.legacy`. Help pages are the reference, and this one is worth reading once.
